newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Despite volcano, lanterns glow in Philippine town.
newsitem.headline: Despite volcano, lanterns glow in Philippine town.

text.p: Despite lingering threats of mudflows from nearby Mount Pinatubo volcano, the lanterns of Christmas glowed as bright as ever this weekend in this town north of Manila.

To the pounding of martial hymns, the strains of Tchaikovsky's piano concerto and the earthy beat of macarena music, what are perhaps the world's biggest lanterns were lit up on Friday in an orgy of colours, lights and songs.
"It won't be Christmas in San Fernando without them," festival organiser Cleofe David said, referring to the six-metre (18-foot) tall lanterns illuminated by up to 5,000 lightbulbs.
"Whatever happens, there will always be these giant lanterns."
In October last year, walls of mud from Pinatubo buried dozens of houses in San Fernando, about 40 km (65 miles) north of Manila, forcing 40,000 villagers to flee for their lives.

Scientists say more than 20 million tonnes of hot rocks and ashes still lie on Pinatubo's slopes, five years after it erupted in one of the century's biggest volcanic blasts, and that mudflows will remain a major threat to nearby towns beyond the year 2000.

The December lantern festival in San Fernando, Pampanga Province, is one of the high points of Yuletide celebrations in the Philippines, Asia's only Catholic-dominated nation and which has perhaps the longest Christmas season in the world.
Carols extolling a white Christmas in a tropical country that has never seen snow start ringing out from radio stations as early as September.
Weeks of frenzied buying start in October when thousands of Filipinos descend on stores offering up to 75 percent discounts in "midnight madness" pre-Christmas sales lasting deep into the night.
Street urchins grab the show two weeks before Christmas day.

In a uniquely Filipino method of carolling, they make rounds of their neighbourhoods every night until New Year's Day, banging tin cans and singing songs until householders part with a small monetary gift.
Organised choir groups, usually composed of students and young professionals, fare better, collecting a few thousand pesos a night by serenading politicians or businessmen.
The more conservative Filipinos celebrate by attending nine straight pre-dawn masses from December 16 to Christmas eve, topped by a midnight mass on the night of December 24.

Christmas eve for most is a time for family reunions. At the stroke of midnight, grandparents, parents, children and grandchildren gather around tables heaped with food for the traditional "noche buena" or midnight repast.
After the customary exchange of gifts on Christmas Day, street carols last until the first Sunday of January when the Christmas season officially ends by the Catholic calendar.
It is also the time when small paper lanterns and strings of Christmas lights hung on windows or doorways of the humblest of Filipino homes are brought down.
It is the time, too, when the lanterns of San Fernando are dismantled and put away in boxes to await another Christmas.

Many Filipinos see the frenzied celebrations at Christmas time as a celebration of life amid the vagaries of nature that the Philippines is prone to. For much of the year, the country is lashed by typhoons and floods.
Earthquakes are frequent occurrences.
"We feel this is a unifying force," said San Fernando mayor Rey Aquino of the lantern festival.
"No matter what the hardships...the lanterns of San Fernando will never dim."
